newsitem.title: UK: IPE Brent tests support, gas oil off but stable.
newsitem.headline: IPE Brent tests support, gas oil off but stable.

text.p: IPE Brent crude futures briefly dipped through key support at $19.75 but were bounced back buy good buying at the level. Gas oil futures held steady at the lower levels after sustaining early losses, brokers said.

A firm bed of support on the July Brent contract around $19.75 a barrel, last Wednesday's low, was briefly broken as the market gapped down to $19.70 in early Tuesday trade, but the marked gapped up equally as quickly to next trade at $19.76.
At 1137 GMT the July Brent contract stood 25 cents a barrel lower at $19.75 a barrel. June gas oil was $2 a tonne lower at $175.75, 50 cents up from the session low.
Brokers said crude will be looking ahead to this week's U.S. inventory data to determine whether demand in unleaded gasoline will lend enough support to lead prices in the short term.
With peak demand season for unleaded gasoline at hand from last weekend's unofficial beginning of summer in the U.S., crude oil should be taking a back seat but demand for gasoline remains slow.

"We are now supposedly in the driving season and although gasoline stocks are still millions of barrels lower than this time last year the traditional pre-summer bull rally has not materialised," said Fenella Graham at MeesPierson Derivatives.

"The problem of looking at gasoline as a guide for the crude market is that the gasoline crack spread has recently been very low and therefore gasoline prices can afford to rally without too much of a pull on the crudes," Graham added.
American Petroleum Institute (API) data released last week showed U.S. gasoline stocks rose by 800,000 barrels but were still nearly seven million barrels below year ago levels.

Narrow crack margins for products has led to some refiners in Asia and Europe cutting back crude runs. Analysts said this combined with maintenance turnarounds could start to put some pressure on crude prices.
The general lack of momentum was also seen keeping crude markets on the defensive for a while.
Shell has cut crude throughput at its 350,000 barrel per day Pernis refinery in Rotterdam by "roughly 14 percent" due to poor operating margins, trade sources said on Tuesday.
Shell's move followed similar cuts at Texaco and BP's Nerefco complex last week.
Refiners in Europe have had their profit margins decimated by the recent sharp rise in crude price, which has not been matched by an equally strong rise in the value of oil products.

According to Reuters calculations using standard yields, a complex European refinery is now making just over a $1 profit for every barrel of crude processed. A simple refinery in Europe is losing 30 cents on each barrel.
